topics.label: AI Literacy & Capability
topics.description: Critical capabilities needed to become AI fluent — frameworks, competencies, and workforce readiness.

articles.title: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health - Nature
articles.snippet: A competency framework for digital public health in Europe: an updated scoping review | npj Digital Public Health  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on European digital public health contexts; findings may have limited applicability to non-European healthcare systems with different regulatory frameworks, funding structures, and workforce development approaches.
takeaways: Use the competency framework to identify priority skill gaps in your digital health workforce — map current capabilities against the framework to target upskilling efforts where impact will be highest.

Adopt a structured approach to AI literacy for public health professionals by anchoring training to validated competencies rather than generic tech skills, ensuring relevance to healthcare delivery and policy contexts.

Consider how the European framework aligns (or conflicts) with your organisation's current digital capability maturity; this can inform whether you need to adapt frameworks or develop context-specific competency models.

articles.title: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education - Nature
articles.snippet: Integration of artificial intelligence competencies into a holistic digital literacy framework for middle school education  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on middle school education context; applicability to workplace AI literacy development and adult learning environments would require adaptation.
takeaways: AI competencies should be embedded within a broader digital literacy framework rather than taught in isolation, creating connections between technical skills, critical thinking, and ethical understanding.
Middle school represents a critical development stage for foundational AI literacy; similar scaffolded approaches may help adult learners build confidence before engaging with complex AI tools.

A holistic framework emphasizes not just 'how to use AI' but understanding AI's societal impact and limitations — this mindset matters as much as technical competency for employees navigating AI in the workplace.

articles.title: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health - Frontiers
articles.snippet: From resistance to readiness: faculty development as the key to AI literacy in public health  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — focuses on faculty development in public health education context; findings may not generalise to other sectors or non-academic settings. Geographic scope unclear from title/snippet.
takeaways: Faculty development programmes can shift employee mindsets from AI resistance to readiness; consider designing structured learning pathways that address concerns and build confidence rather than mandating adoption.

In knowledge-intensive professions (like public health), upskilling educators or senior staff first creates a cascading effect — they then model AI literacy for colleagues and teams, improving organisational readiness.
Addressing psychological barriers (resistance, anxiety, scepticism) through targeted development is as important as technical training when rolling out AI literacy initiatives.

articles.title: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Strategies for developing AI competencies in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on higher education sector; applicability to workplace AI literacy development may require contextual adaptation beyond academic settings.
takeaways: Identify which AI competencies are most critical for your organisation's roles, then map these to structured learning pathways rather than ad-hoc training.
Consider blended approaches combining technical skill-building with critical thinking about AI limitations and ethical use — not just 'how to use' but 'when and why'.
Design competency development with clear progression levels so employees can build foundational understanding before tackling advanced applications relevant to their work.

articles.title: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy as a meta-skill: a four-domain model for academic management innovation in higher education  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — framework-based conceptual model for higher education; applicability to corporate learning and development contexts requires adaptation, and geographic scope is unclear from snippet.
takeaways: Use a multi-domain model of AI literacy (likely technical, critical, ethical, and applied domains) rather than viewing it as a single skill — this helps design targeted capability-building programs for different employee roles and levels.

Position AI literacy as a 'meta-skill' that enables people to learn other capabilities — emphasise how foundational AI understanding accelerates adoption of specific AI tools and organisational innovation.

Adapt the four-domain framework to your organisational context by mapping which domains matter most for different teams (e.g. technical teams may need deeper technical literacy; management may prioritise strategic and ethical domains).

articles.title: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI literacy in undergraduate medical education: a competency-based interpretive framework for curriculum and assessment  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Moderate — focuses on medical education context specifically. The competency framework may have limited direct application to non-medical workplace AI literacy programmes, though principles could be adapted.
takeaways: Use a competency-based framework when designing AI literacy programmes — clearly map the knowledge, skills, and attitudes needed rather than treating AI literacy as generic technical training.

Consider assessment methods that test applied competencies (e.g. case-based scenarios, critical appraisal tasks) rather than only theoretical knowledge, to ensure learning transfers to workplace decisions.

Structure curriculum around contextual use cases (in medicine: diagnostic support, clinical decision-making) rather than AI technology in isolation — this increases relevance and engagement in professional settings.

topics.label: AI & Organisational Psychology
topics.description: Impact of AI on wellbeing, engagement, job crafting, trust, and other org psych constructs.

articles.title: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The double-edged mechanism of organizational AI adoption on employee creativity  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Cannot assess without access to full article — snippet provides only title and journal name. Generalisability depends on study design, sample size, geographic scope, and sector representation, which are not evident from the title alone.
takeaways: AI adoption in organisations can have conflicting effects on creativity — some conditions may enhance creative thinking while others may constrain it; leaders should map which specific AI implementations risk stifling creativity before rollout.

Design AI tools and workflows with employee creativity in mind, not just efficiency; consider whether automation of routine tasks actually frees cognitive capacity for innovation, or whether it narrows problem-solving scope.

Monitor creativity metrics alongside productivity metrics when rolling out AI — the 'double-edged' framing suggests trade-offs exist that require active management to prevent unintended creative suppression.

articles.title: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership - Nature
articles.snippet: Organizational psychological ownership drives employee-AI collaboration via AI crafting under paternalistic leadership  Nature
articles.generalisability: Unclear from snippet alone — findings may be limited by geographic and cultural scope (paternalistic leadership is culturally contingent). Generalisability to non-paternalistic or Western management contexts requires verification.
takeaways: Foster psychological ownership of AI tools among employees by involving them in customising and shaping how AI is integrated into their workflows — this can enhance collaboration regardless of leadership style.

Under paternalistic leadership structures, emphasise mentorship and protective guidance when introducing AI; this approach may amplify willingness to engage with and adapt AI tools to individual work contexts.

Design AI adoption programmes that create space for 'AI crafting' — allowing employees to modify or personalise AI features — as a pathway to deeper buy-in and collaborative use rather than passive acceptance.

articles.title: The Psychological Costs of Adopting AI - Harvard Business Review
articles.snippet: The Psychological Costs of Adopting AI  Harvard Business Review
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Harvard Business Review articles typically draw on broad organizational experience but lack specific empirical data on sample composition, geography, or sector representation. Findings likely generalizable to knowledge workers in developed economies, but applicability to other contexts unclear.
takeaways: Identify and monitor psychological stressors specific to AI adoption in your workplace—such as job security anxiety, skill obsolescence concerns, or increased workload during transition—rather than assuming uniform impact across teams.

Design targeted psychological support interventions (e.g., reskilling programs, transparent communication about role changes, peer support networks) to mitigate adoption-related distress and maintain employee wellbeing during AI implementation.

Assess baseline psychological safety and trust in your organization before rolling out AI tools; organizations with low psychological safety may experience amplified anxiety and resistance, requiring more intensive change management.

articles.title: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox - Frontiers
articles.snippet: The effects of generative AI usage on employee knowledge behavior: a perspective based on the Automation–Augmentation Paradox  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — article snippet does not provide sufficient information about sample size, geographic scope, industry sectors, or methodology to assess how broadly findings apply.
takeaways: Generative AI adoption may create a paradox where automation of routine tasks paradoxically reduces employee engagement with knowledge-building activities; consider designing interventions that require workers to actively synthesize AI outputs rather than passively consume them.

Monitor whether increased AI usage leads to skill atrophy in knowledge work (e.g., research, analysis, writing); establish feedback loops to ensure employees remain knowledge-builders, not just AI supervisors.

articles.title: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study - Nature
articles.snippet: Work autonomy mediates associations between medical AI readiness and well being in a three wave nurse study  Nature
articles.generalisability: Findings apply specifically to nursing contexts where medical AI is being implemented. Generalisability to other professions or healthcare settings unclear without access to full methodology. Three-wave design strengthens causal inference but sample characteristics and geographic scope require verification.
takeaways: To support nurse wellbeing during AI adoption, actively preserve and expand work autonomy — don't let AI implementation reduce nurses' decision-making authority or control over their tasks, as autonomy is the key mechanism linking readiness to wellbeing.

Frame AI readiness programs not just as technical training, but as conversations about how AI will enhance (not replace) nurses' professional judgment and independent practice; this psychological framing influences wellbeing outcomes over time.

articles.title: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression - PsyPost
articles.snippet: Psychological safety mediates link between AI adoption and worker depression  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Generalisability unclear — snippet provides insufficient detail on sample size, geographic scope, sector, and methodology. Full article review needed to assess whether findings apply broadly across industries and regions.
takeaways: Create explicit psychological safety protocols before or alongside AI tool rollouts — workers who feel safe to voice concerns and ask questions about AI are less likely to experience depression-related outcomes during adoption.
Monitor mental health and wellbeing during AI transitions, particularly for teams reporting low psychological safety; targeted support may prevent downstream negative mental health effects.
Frame AI adoption conversations around worker capability and learning rather than replacement risk — this helps maintain trust and psychological safety during technology change.

topics.label: Behavioural Change Frameworks
topics.description: Evidence-based frameworks for driving behaviour change — in the context of AI adoption and workforce transformation.

articles.title: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI - Deloitte
articles.snippet: AI adoption to adaptation: How a new change approach can build the human behaviors needed for AI  Deloitte
articles.generalisability: Moderate — Deloitte practitioner perspective likely based on consulting experience, but without explicit sample data, geographic scope, or sector specification, applicability varies by organisational context.
takeaways: Shift from 'AI adoption' framing to 'AI adaptation' — this reframes change as building new behaviours rather than simply implementing technology, which can help teams focus on capability development alongside tool implementation.

Use structured change approaches (likely drawing on organisational psychology principles) to target the human behaviours that enable AI use, rather than assuming adoption follows automatically from access to tools.

Tailor behavioural change interventions to your workforce's readiness and role-specific needs — adaptation success depends on how well you build capability in the specific behaviours your people need, not just training on features.

articles.title: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Dual-path mechanism of AI awareness on employee job crafting: insights from the cognitive appraisal of stress and JD-R perspective | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Moderate — study applies cognitive appraisal theory and Job Demands-Resources framework, but generalisability depends on sample composition (size, sectors, geographies) not evident from title/snippet alone.
takeaways: Help employees reframe AI as a resource rather than a threat by facilitating cognitive reappraisal conversations — this dual-path approach (stress perception and job redesign) can shift how workers adapt their roles when AI is introduced.

When implementing AI tools, create structured opportunities for job crafting — allowing employees to proactively reshape their tasks and responsibilities reduces anxiety and enables them to leverage AI awareness productively.

articles.title: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work - Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.snippet: How AI is Reshaping the Future of Work  Stanford Graduate School of Business
articles.generalisability: Limited — Stanford GSB perspective on AI and work trends; lacks empirical data or specific geographic scope. Findings reflect US business school viewpoint and may not account for regulatory, cultural, or economic differences in other regions including Australia.
takeaways: Identify specific roles and tasks in your organisation where AI adoption is most feasible, then design targeted change communication that frames AI as a tool augmenting (not replacing) employee capabilities to reduce resistance.

Establish feedback loops with frontline staff early in AI implementation to surface real concerns about workflow disruption, which can be addressed proactively rather than becoming barriers to adoption later.

articles.title: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective - Frontiers
articles.snippet: How does organizational AI adoption affect employees’ job crafting behaviors? An approach-avoidance perspective  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: Limited — sample characteristics and geographic scope not evident from title and snippet; findings may vary significantly depending on organizational context, industry sector, and employee demographics.
takeaways: AI adoption can trigger divergent employee responses: some employees may actively reshape their roles to work alongside AI (approach), while others may withdraw or avoid AI-related tasks (avoidance) — managers should assess which response pattern is emerging in their teams and intervene accordingly.

Understanding the psychological mechanisms behind approach-avoidance behavior during AI adoption enables targeted interventions (e.g., skills training, role redesign, psychological safety initiatives) to encourage constructive job crafting rather than disengagement.

Monitor how AI implementation influences employees' voluntary role adjustments early; proactive job crafting discussions can help employees reframe their roles positively rather than defaulting to avoidance strategies.

articles.title: AI-induced job crafting: a systematic review of cognitive appraisal pathways - Frontiers
articles.snippet: AI-induced job crafting: a systematic review of cognitive appraisal pathways  Frontiers
articles.generalisability: High — systematic review synthesises findings across multiple studies and geographies, though generalisability depends on the quality and diversity of included primary studies.
takeaways: Help employees reframe AI adoption as an opportunity to reshape their roles rather than a threat — focus coaching on how they can use AI to eliminate routine tasks and redirect energy toward higher-value work.

Understand that cognitive appraisal (how employees interpret the meaning of AI) is the critical lever for behaviour change — employees who see AI as enhancing their capabilities are more likely to actively redesign their jobs than those who see it as replacement.

Design interventions that target the appraisal process early in AI rollout, such as skills workshops and peer stories, rather than waiting for negative interpretations to take hold and require remediation.

articles.title: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: Challenge or threat? The double-edged sword effect of AI use on innovative teaching behavior among primary and secondary school teachers in China | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Limited to Chinese primary and secondary school contexts; findings may not generalise to other educational systems with different institutional structures, teacher training models, or cultural attitudes toward technology adoption.
takeaways: AI adoption can paradoxically inhibit innovative teaching if framed as a threat to professional autonomy or job security; reframe AI as a tool that enhances rather than replaces teacher expertise to unlock positive behaviour change.

Teachers' psychological response to AI (viewing it as a challenge vs. threat) is a critical lever for driving innovation adoption — invest in messaging, support, and training that emphasises capability development and professional growth opportunities.
When introducing AI tools in educational settings, proactively address anxiety and resistance through clear communication about how AI augments teaching practice rather than diminishing it.

topics.label: Fascinating Psychology Research
topics.description: Surprising, counterintuitive, and delightful findings from personality and behaviour research — the kind of study you'd share at dinner.

articles.title: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism - PsyPost
articles.snippet: New psychology research shows the surprising romantic advantage of antagonistic narcissism  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unable to assess without access to the underlying research — news snippet does not provide sufficient detail on sample size, geographic scope, or methodology.
takeaways: Antagonistic narcissism (dominance-seeking, confrontational traits) may paradoxically boost short-term romantic attraction, despite the personality type typically being associated with relationship toxicity.

The finding challenges the intuitive assumption that kindness and humility are universally attractive — some people may be drawn to assertiveness and confidence even when paired with antagonistic traits.
This highlights how evolutionary psychology can reveal mismatches between what we think we want in partners and what actually triggers attraction at a biological level.

articles.title: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality - PsyPost
articles.snippet: An AI analyzed wine reviews and found a surprising link to personality  PsyPost
articles.generalisability: Unclear — snippet provides minimal methodological detail. Generalisability depends on the size and diversity of the wine review sample analysed, which is not described.
takeaways: Language patterns in casual writing (like wine reviews) can reveal personality traits — suggesting your word choices say more about you than you might think.
AI can detect subtle personality signals in everyday text, opening intriguing possibilities for understanding people through their natural communication rather than formal assessments.
Wine tasting notes are apparently a window into personality, making this a fun reminder that hobbies and preferences often reveal who we are in unexpected ways.

articles.snippet: When artificial intelligence becomes a job resource: how psychological capital fuels innovation in algorithm-driven workplaces  Frontiers

articles.title: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025 - PwC
articles.snippet: Global Workforce Hopes and Fears Survey 2025  PwC
articles.generalisability: Moderate to high — PwC surveys typically reach large samples across multiple countries and sectors, though specific sample composition and weighting methods would need verification. Results reflect workforce sentiment at a particular moment and may not capture longer-term patterns.
takeaways: Identify which psychological safety concerns (e.g., fear of job displacement, anxiety about skill relevance, concerns about speaking up) are most prevalent in your workforce — use survey findings to benchmark your organisation's psychological safety gaps against global peers.

Use the 'hopes' data to understand what conditions employees believe would foster trust and belonging — design targeted interventions (e.g., transparent communication about AI adoption, upskilling programs, inclusive decision-making) that directly address these aspirations.

Monitor how psychological safety concerns vary by demographics, role level, and industry sector within the data — tailor your psychological safety initiatives rather than applying a one-size-fits-all approach.

articles.title: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams - Frontiers
articles.snippet: Algorithmic inclusion? The role of AI-assisted inclusive leadership in shaping gendered outcomes in multicultural academic teams  Frontiers
articles.sample: Academic teams (geographic scope not specified in snippet)
articles.generalisability: Limited — findings are specific to multicultural academic teams and may not generalise to other sectors, industries, or organisational contexts. The snippet does not clarify sample size or geographic distribution.
takeaways: AI tools can be leveraged to support inclusive leadership practices, potentially helping leaders recognise and mitigate unconscious gendered biases in team dynamics and decision-making.

In multicultural academic settings, algorithmic support for inclusion may help surface overlooked voices and ensure equitable participation — consider piloting structured AI-assisted check-ins to monitor team psychological safety and representation by gender and cultural background.

Psychological safety in diverse teams may improve when leaders use AI insights to track whose contributions are being heard and valued, helping prevent gendered patterns of exclusion or marginalisation.

articles.title: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications - Nature
articles.snippet: The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership | Humanities and Social Sciences Communications  Nature
articles.generalisability: Generalisability depends on the study's sample size and sector coverage, which are not evident from the title and snippet. The causal pathway (AI adoption → reduced psychological safety → depression) requires verification across different organisational contexts and geographies before broad application.
takeaways: AI adoption can inadvertently undermine psychological safety if not accompanied by explicit ethical leadership practices — leaders must actively communicate AI's purpose, acknowledge concerns, and model ethical decision-making to protect employee wellbeing.
Monitor employee mental health outcomes (depression, anxiety) during and after AI implementation; psychological safety should be a leading indicator tracked alongside technical adoption metrics.

When rolling out AI tools, prioritise transparent communication about how decisions are made, who is accountable, and how employees can voice concerns without fear — this buffers against the negative mental health effects the research identifies.

articles.title: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees - Boston Consulting Group
articles.snippet: Psychological Safety Levels the Playing Field for Employees  Boston Consulting Group
articles.generalisability: Moderate — BCG research typically draws from global client work and surveys, but specific sample composition, size, and methodology are not detailed in the snippet provided. Findings likely apply broadly to large organisations but may be less relevant for small teams or non-corporate settings.
takeaways: Create explicit norms and practices that signal psychological safety — such as inviting dissent in meetings, acknowledging mistakes visibly, and protecting people from retaliation — to level access to voice and participation across hierarchy and background.
Measure psychological safety alongside inclusion metrics; teams that feel safe to speak up are more likely to surface diverse perspectives and challenge groupthink, improving decision quality.

Train managers to model vulnerability and curiosity rather than omniscience — this shifts the dynamic from 'prove yourself' to 'we're learning together,' making it safer for quieter or underrepresented employees to contribute.
